question: Let \(p\) and \(q\) be positive integers such that \[ \dfrac{5}{9}\lt\dfrac{p}{q}\lt\dfrac{4}{7} \] and \(q\) is as small as possible. What is \(q-p?\)
solution:
The strict inequalities create positive integer gaps, and each such gap must be at least \(1\). Cross-multiplying gives
\[
9p-5q\ge1,
\qquad 4q-7p\ge1.
\]
The distance between the two bounding fractions equals the sum of the distances from \(p/q\) to those bounds. Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac1{63}
&=\frac47-\frac59\\
&=\left(\frac pq-\frac59\right)+\left(\frac47-\frac pq\right)\\
&=\frac{9p-5q}{9q}+\frac{4q-7p}{7q}\\
&\ge\frac1{9q}+\frac1{7q}
=\frac{16}{63q}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Multiplying by \(63q>0\) shows that \(q\ge16\).

For \(q=16\), the required numerator satisfies
\[
\frac{80}{9}<p<\frac{64}{7}.
\]
This interval lies inside \((8,10)\) and contains \(9\), since \(80<81\) and \(63<64\). Thus its only integer is \(p=9\), and \(9/16\) attains the smallest possible denominator.

Therefore
\[
q-p=16-9=\boxed7.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
